_about: THE DARK KNIGHT SAMPLE'S SCREENPLAY - 40 scenes, the pages the rest of
the sample is derived from.
A RECONSTRUCTION FOR PRACTICE. It follows the public structure of the
film scene by scene; every action line and every line of dialogue is
newly written for this app, and every piece of paperwork around it is
invented. It is not the film's screenplay and none of the film's famous
lines appear in it. No real cast or crew is named anywhere.
WHY IT IS ITS OWN FILE. sample.darkknight.json is a static import, so
every byte of it sits in first paint; these pages are bigger than the
whole of the rest of that file and are needed only after a click, so the
hub reaches them with a dynamic import and they ship as their own chunk,
with the matching exception in vite.config.js, as Dragon's do.
WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM. scenes[].eighths and pageNumber in
sample.darkknight.json are MEASURED off these pages by
scripts/make-sample-darkknight.mjs with script.js's own metric
(LINES_PER_PAGE = 55, action 61 columns, dialogue 35), so the breakdown,
the schedule and the budget cannot disagree with the pages. The headings
are generated from the scene rows, so they match them in count and order.
Edit the scene sources in scripts/sample-darkknight/ and regenerate; do
not edit this file by hand.

elements.text: SAMPLE PAGES. This screenplay was written for this app, as the pages its demo project is broken down from. It is a reconstruction for practice: it follows the public structure of The Dark Knight (2008) scene by scene, but every action line and every line of dialogue is newly written here, and all of the paperwork attached to it is invented, imagined as if a Chennai unit were making the film. It is not the film's screenplay and contains none of its dialogue. Delete the project, or edit any of it, and nothing is lost.

The dialogue is in English and the slug lines, action and transitions are too, which is the arrangement a screenplay page needs for its fixed-width Courier grid to stay arithmetic: this app's schedule, sides and budget are all derived from that count. The locations are Chennai and Tamil Nadu stand-ins, all invented.
Morning light on a wide street of shopfronts. A yellow school bus idles at the kerb in front of the CO-OPERATIVE BANK, one wheel up on the pavement.
The bank's shutters are half raised. A watchman sweeps the step with a broom that has lost most of its bristles.
Inside the bus, four men sit in a row. Overalls, gloves, canvas bags between their boots.
TALL MASK checks his watch. STOUT MASK checks a shotgun he has already checked twice.
The DRIVER does not check anything. He watches the bank's front door in the mirror.
Four minutes past. Manager comes in at ten past.
Because the man who told me has a cousin there, and the cousin is never on time but always ten past.
Then we have a longer morning.
The fourth man sits by the window. He has not spoken. He holds a rubber clown mask in his lap and turns it over like a fruit he is deciding whether to buy.
Somebody who works for the man who planned it.
Planned what? The man who planned it is not here.
The quiet man puts the mask on. The face underneath is gone. In its place, a wide painted grin that was never meant to be friendly.
He is the JOKER. He stands, bag over his shoulder, and steps down off the bus like a man getting off at his own stop.
The others pull on their masks. A school bag lies forgotten on the seat behind them. Nobody touches it.
The watchman looks up from his broom as four grinning faces come across the pavement toward him.
He opens his mouth. The Joker lifts a gloved finger to his own lips, politely.
The watchman sits down on the step. The broom lies across his knees. The four go in over him.
Across the road a tea-seller sees it all and, with the calm of a man who has seen worse, pulls his shutter down halfway and goes on stirring.
A schoolboy in a blue uniform stops on the corner, looks at the bus, looks at the bank, and decides to take the long way to class.
The bank hall. Ceiling fans, a long counter, twelve CUSTOMERS in two queues. The doors bang open.
Everybody down. Phones on the floor, hands on your heads, nobody is brave this morning.
Customers drop to the tiles. A clerk puts both hands up so high he knocks his own nameplate over.
STOUT MASK runs the length of the counter, sweeping cash trays into a bag. The BANK MANAGER comes out of a back office, grey with a long career of never being surprised.
Do you understand whose money this is? These are pensioners' savings.
Then they will be glad to hear where they are going.
The manager reaches under the desk. A shotgun blast takes the panel off the desk. The manager falls back through his own door.
The Joker does not turn. He watches the vault door.
Driver is cutting the alarm line now.
Good. Go and give him a hand. Take the little one.
Tall Mask hesitates, then nods at Stout Mask. The two go out through a side door. The Joker is alone with the customers and the ceiling fans.
He crouches by a young woman face down on the tiles.
Be uncomfortable if you like. Nobody will mind.
A shot behind the counter. The thud of a body. The Joker straightens.
Tall Mask comes back through the side door, bag on one shoulder, shotgun swinging.
He is finished. The driver is finished. That was the plan, yes?
Almost every plan has a line in it that says one man is finished. Yours had a second line.
The Joker's hand drifts under his coat. Tall Mask looks down.
You said it was a small share, but a share.
I did. I said it to the others as well.
A single shot. Tall Mask folds against the counter.
The vault door stands open on rows of tied bundles. The Joker takes a bag from the dead man's shoulder, then a second bag, and a third.
Stout Mask stumbles back in from the side door with a bleeding arm.
It was the driver. He shot the other one. I came to tell you...
He sees the dead man at the counter. He understands where his own place is in the line.
Wait, wait. I was only the one who carried things.
That is a very dangerous job. You have done it very well.
A shot. The customers cringe as one body.
The Joker slings three bags across his back. He passes the manager's office, glances in.
The manager lies against the wall, alive and furious, a hand pressed to his side.
You will never spend a single rupee of it. They will find you.
I am not worried about spending. I am worried about the weekend.
He kneels, tucks a folded card into the manager's top pocket and pats it flat.
Show it to your friends. It lists the services that we offer.
The Joker walks to the door and out. The customers listen to the school bus pulling away.
Then the alarm bell begins, a full minute late. It rings and rings over a hall full of people lying still.
Night. A rooftop above Anna Salai, high enough that the traffic is a murmur. A big searchlight with a bat-shaped cut-out stands bolted to the roof, switched off.
GORDON stands beside it in his overcoat, a thermos in one hand and a folder in the other. RAMIREZ waits near the stairwell door, watching the sky.
Commissioner says you are not to be out here without a team, sir.
The Commissioner has never told me where to be at night. I enjoy it.
Wait on the stairs. Come up if there is shouting, or if it starts to rain.
Ramirez goes. Gordon switches on the searchlight. The beam climbs, and in the cloud a bat shape forms.
He pours tea into the thermos lid, takes a sip. A shadow separates itself from the tower behind him.
BATMAN stands at the edge, ten feet away. He has been there some time.
Then you know why I have asked you here.
Gordon opens the folder on the parapet and spreads out three photographs under a paperweight.
Three men in the past week. All dressed as you. All carrying hockey sticks.
They think they are. One of them lost two fingers to a dog. Another is in a coma.
Because the real thing has stopped coming out in daylight and they would like to see it done. People do not want a legend. They want a standard.
A silence. The beam turns lazily across the rooftop.
And that is only half of it. Somebody has put a price on the mob's accounts.
Dent's. We have a judge who will sign what he writes. There is only one problem.
Faster than the paper. Every account we lifted was emptied the day before.
Someone is warning them. Or somebody is moving it for them.
Find me the one who moves it.
Heaven forbid. Bring him wherever you like, as long as he can speak when he arrives.
Batman considers the photographs. One of the imitators wears a welder's mask, taped at the edges.
These men need to be found before they are hurt.
Gordon lets out a short laugh and pours the last of the tea out over the parapet.
You cannot guard anyone without being seen. And you cannot be seen.
That is the problem I came here to solve.
He goes to the edge. The searchlight beam passes over him and leaves only the cloud.
Gordon turns. The rooftop is empty. The beam sweeps on.
A chemical depot at the edge of the city. Rusted drums stacked in rows, a gantry across the front, one sodium light buzzing over a yard of wet concrete.
A tanker lorry backs in. Two vans follow. Eleven men in leather jackets get down, GAMBOL at their head, a short thick man with a shaving cut on his chin.
In the middle of the yard, kneeling on the ground with their hands behind their heads, are two men in homemade armour. Bin lids, cricket pads, a welder's mask taped on.
And who told you to go through my people's shipment?
We were not going through it. We were just standing in front of it.
We thought it would be frightening.
Gambol looks at one of his men. A man tosses him an iron pipe.
It was a fine idea. It was only badly executed.
He raises the pipe. A sodium light overhead goes out with a bright crack.
The yard drops into darkness. Somebody laughs, nervous. Another light dies, and another.
A thud. A man falls past the tanker. Another is hoisted into the gantry and does not come down.
Gambol backs away between the drums, pipe held high. A shape steps out of the dark in front of him.
Batman. He takes the pipe in one hand and folds it in the middle like a piece of paper.
A fist; the wall behind Gambol rings. The remaining men rush together. Batman is among them, quick and unglamorous, making each blow count and no more.
The imitators stay kneeling, hands still behind their heads, watching a master do what they had pretended to do.
Batman pins Gambol against a drum and holds him there with one arm.
Who moves your money after you are through here?
I do not know any bankers.
You know where the vans go from here.
To a place near the harbour. A man there counts it. Then it goes overseas.
Lau. That is all I have. They do not tell us anything else.
Batman lets go and Gambol slides down the drum. A police siren, very far off.
He turns to the imitators. They get up carefully, pads rattling.
Sir, we only wanted to help.
I know. You will help more by staying home.
But if we were to just practise a little...
Take the suits off. Go home. Tell nobody.
He steps back into the shadows. The two men look at each other, then at the empty place where he stood. Slowly, they begin to unbuckle the bin lids.
INT. WAYNE ENTERPRISES TOWER, GUINDY - DAY
Morning. A tall tower of glass and steel at Guindy, its lobby full of office workers carrying cardboard cups.
Inside, on the forty-second floor, a quiet corridor leads to a glass-walled laboratory. BRUCE WAYNE walks in, jacket over one arm, tie loosened.
FOX looks up from a bench. He wears a cardigan with one button missing and half-moon glasses pushed up into thin hair.
You are early. I have had a policy for twenty years against being surprised before ten.
I wanted to see the new panel.
It is a good panel. It is also on loan from a part of the company I wish you would stop visiting.
He lifts a charcoal-coloured plate the size of a dinner tray and sets it on the bench. Bruce runs a thumb along the edge.
It will stop a knife and it will stop a thrown car door and it will not stop you from going where you should not go. Please do not try the last one.
People always wear it too long.
Bruce smiles. He sets the panel down gently, then looks at a second sheet pinned to the glass. Rows of numbers in columns, some highlighted in yellow.
Something I should have shown you last week. A depositor list from a small bank I look after on the side.
Fourteen accounts in different names whose balances rise on the same day, to the rupee, and fall on the same day. They belong to somebody who is careful.
I do not know. But when a person is that careful, there is a man behind them who does the careful part.
An accountant in the oldest sense. A man who makes the dirty thing clean and then goes home to dinner.
Bruce stares at the column of numbers.
Where do the balances end up?
Across the sea. A firm in the east. They have an office on one of the high floors of a new tower, and they keep it very nicely.
How long has the firm been there?
Eight months. They hold a great deal of money.
Mr Wayne, a visit to a firm like that is not a visit. It is a deposit.
Then I will make a deposit.
Fox takes off his glasses and polishes them carefully on his cardigan.
I will arrange the introduction. I would like to say for the record that I did not enjoy it.
Bruce picks up the panel again. This time he holds it against his shoulder, like a man trying on a coat.
And you will not wear that one.
A courtroom in an old building, brown wood and brass fans, packed to the doors. A heavy rain taps against the high windows.
HARVEY DENT stands before the witness box, jacket off, sleeves turned back twice. He is calm in the way people are when they have already won.
In the dock, MARONI sits between two lawyers, a large man in a silk shirt with a gold chain. He watches Dent with half-closed eyes.
A WITNESS, the book-keeper, sits very still in the box.
You kept the shop's accounts for six years.
And in those six years you never saw a payment from a person called Maroni.
Never in cash. Never by cheque. Never in a plain envelope left on a Friday.
I did not say that, sir.
I said I did not see a payment from a person with that name.
I see. And the envelope on Fridays, who was that from?
Does the friend have a name?
He is only ever called the friend.
RACHEL rises at the prosecution table and hands him a small card. He holds it up to the court.
This is a card from the printing house on Mint Street. It says on the back, in your handwriting, that sixty envelopes were bought in this man's name. Is that your hand?
The witness looks at the card. A long moment. His eyes slide, helplessly, to the dock.
Maroni does not move. He only smiles.
You do not need to look at him. He cannot help you now.
Objection. My lord, my learned friend is badgering.
I would call it vigorous. Overruled. Mr Dent, you are on the edge of a long speech.
I am nearly finished, my lord.
Dent turns to the jury. He takes a coin from his waistcoat and runs it across his knuckles without looking at it.

Members of the jury, a man who keeps accounts for six years knows exactly how much money has passed through his hands. He is asking you to believe he never saw the largest part of it. Ask yourselves why he says that.
The coin disappears into his palm.
He says it because he is afraid. Not of me. Of a man who is in this room and who will not be able to reach him tonight.
Silence. In the dock, Maroni's smile does not change.
Then a sudden movement in the gallery. A juror's fan falls to the floor. The Judge strikes the bench.
Order. Order. We will adjourn for ten minutes and Mr Dent will remember that a gallery is not a jury.
The court breaks up. Dent steps back from the box and finds Maroni standing beside him, close, large, quiet.
Everybody likes a show, Mr Dent. Even people in my line.
Then you will like the verdict.
I will like it very much. For about a day.
He passes. Rachel watches him go down the aisle, and does not breathe out until he reaches the doors.
He always does. That is why he is still in the dock instead of in a shop.
A heritage hotel in Mylapore, tall wooden doors, brass lamps, candles on every table. A restaurant on the first floor, half full.
At a corner table sit BRUCE WAYNE, RACHEL, and HARVEY DENT. Plates half eaten, a bottle of wine open and unfinished.
I should say before the soup comes cold that I have no interest in your money.
Rachel insisted. She says you are the only man in the city with the sense to ask what it costs.
That is a kind way of saying I am the only one with the money.
I did not say it was a kind way.
Rachel puts down her glass and looks from one to the other.
You two have the same bad habit. You both answer a compliment as if it were a charge.
She is right. I have been trying to stop.
I have a coin. If I fail to take a compliment, I have to pay the coin.
Nobody has ever seen it happen.
He sets the coin flat on the tablecloth. It is old, silver, the face worn nearly smooth.
It is a harmless coin. It has never decided anything.
It has been consulted. It never gives me a straight answer. So I decide on my own and use it to tell the other side I am thinking.
Bruce laughs. It is a real laugh and it surprises him. Rachel looks at him a moment too long, and he looks away.
A WAITER sets down a dessert plate with three spoons.
I have not been so entertained in a restaurant for a year.
You have not been in a restaurant for a year.
I have been in one tonight. You can take my word for what it costs.
A pause. Dent turns the coin over once on his knuckles and tucks it away.
What I want is simple. A city where the person who puts away the guilty is not the one who needs a guard to walk home.
There is a guard already. He has no uniform. I am told he is very inventive.
Bruce picks up his spoon and does not eat.
And you think he can be replaced.
I think he can be retired, when it becomes boring. A city should not depend on a man in a mask. It should depend on a man in a court.
And what if the man in the court has no time?
Then I will ask for more.
Rachel is watching Bruce. He sees it, and the spoon makes a small sound against the plate.
I will help you, Harvey. I will do it in writing.
Thank you. I will not mention it.
He will mention it to everyone.
They laugh. Out the window, rain begins again, soft and steady against the old glass.

A disused spinning mill on the edge of Ambattur. Rows of iron machinery under sheets, high windows painted black. In the middle of the floor, a long trestle table with a laptop and a glass of tea at each place.
Eight men sit round it. MARONI at the head, GAMBOL with a bandage on his chin, THE BROKER, a thin man with spectacles and a cigar that has gone out.
Behind them the great machines stand under dust sheets like a congregation of ghosts. Water drips somewhere into a tin, a patient metronome.
Others stand against the walls. The place smells of oil and old cotton.
I will say this once. Every account we trust has been frozen or emptied.
It is not the prosecutor. A prosecutor is a man with a file. This is a man with a list and he is working his way down it.
Then we make a new list.
Of the people who sign for us. We move the money to places he cannot reach.
They all look at the laptop. On the screen, a window opens. A man in a dark suit sits in a bright office with a glass wall behind him. LAU.
Gentlemen. Good evening. Or good morning, I never get it right.
I have it. All of it. Fourteen accounts, three currencies, safe where nobody asks questions.
I am not a sure man. I am a careful man. It is better.
And if the police come to your door?
They would need to cross the sea first. And to cross the sea they would need a reason that is stronger than politics.
Mr Dent has a court. A court is only a very large room.
Maroni drums his fingers on the table. Somewhere in the mill a pigeon flaps up into the rafters.
By the end of the month, everything is moved. After that, I will not need to take another call from this table.
That is not the answer I wanted.
It is the one I have. Take it or tell me you prefer the old way.
Boxes in cellars. Shopkeepers who count wrong. Men who talk.
Gambol goes quiet. Maroni lets the silence run, then nods once.
End of the month. Send me the numbers on Friday.
I will send them on Thursday. I like to be early.
The window closes. In the mill, a dozen men breathe out at once.
He is very sure for a careful man.
He is on the other side of the sea. Sure is cheap from there.
Police headquarters in Egmore, a Victorian building with a cracked clock over the door. Inside, on the second floor, a long room of ceiling fans and old desks.
On one wall a map of the city is stuck with coloured pins. GORDON stands beside it with a paper cup. HARVEY DENT sits on the edge of a desk, sleeves rolled. RAMIREZ is at the window with a folder.
Fourteen banks, thirty-two accounts. We have the paper for all of them.
If we go at dawn, we are done by noon.
And if the money moves the night before?
Then we do not go at dawn.
Gordon looks at him over the paper cup.
The same warrants, the same banks, the same hour. All of them at once. Whoever tips them off will have no time to spend it.
It is very quick. A judge will want a reason to sign for that.
I know two. One of them will sign if I ask nicely. The other will sign if I tell him he has no choice.
Ramirez smiles. Gordon crosses to the map and moves a pin from a bank in Mylapore to a street corner near the port.
The other thing. Somebody went through that bank yesterday morning wearing masks.
I read the report. Four dead, three of them on the bank's side.
The robbers killed each other. That is an odd robbery.
Some money. A great deal, in fact. And I suspect that it was our money, taken from the people who stole it from us.
By one man who leaves a card.
He takes a small card from his pocket. It is folded in half and ordinary, printed with a smile in cheap purple ink.
It lists services. Cheaper than a lawyer, quicker than an insurer.
Dent turns the card over. On the back, nothing.
I do not think so. I think it is a message to the men whose money it was.
That their money is not a safe thing to be holding.
The door opens. A CONSTABLE brings in three folded warrants and a pen on a string. Dent signs the first in a quick, unreadable hand.
Tonight, then. I will have the judge at his desk by ten.
I will have the men at theirs by eleven.
He scoops the cup from the table, finishes it and drops it in the bin.
And somebody will have to tell the Commissioner before he reads about it.
I do. He looks so tired when he sits.
INT. UNDERGROUND WORKSHOP, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT
A workshop buried under a hillside, a long cavern lit by white work lamps. Racks of dark panels, a workbench, a wall map of the city pinned with red thread.
BRUCE WAYNE stands over the bench in a plain work shirt, sleeves up. FOX is beside him with a cup of tea. ALFRED comes down the stairs carrying a tray.
There is some more of the lemon cake. It is one of the few things I can make without help.
That is the reason I do not enjoy the cake.
He sets the tray on the corner of the bench, beside a mess of wire and a small black box.
Where do I start with a man who is not in this country?
A glass tower. Third floor from the top, east side. An office with a clean desk and nobody sitting at it.
In a room somewhere on that floor. He will have a guard in the corridor and a guard at the stairs and a guard at the lift. He will go home at six.
So you will go in at five fifty.
I will go in at five.
And get out at seven. I think that is the part that wants most of the planning.
Fox holds up the black box. A tiny reel is wound inside it, a thin grey cable.
This will take your weight. It will take two of you, in fact. It will not take two of you plus a guard who is tugging on the other end.
A man with a very large crane.
I will ask the obvious question. How does one rent a crane at nine in the evening without somebody asking what it is for?
One rents it from a firm that has never asked anything in its life.
Bruce takes up the box. He feels the weight of it and the cool length of cable.
The rest is a suit. A better one than the last. A lot of padding, a lot of cloth. A very good fabric from a very bad part of the company.
And a man who says it is all unnecessary.
I say it is all unnecessary. I say it every time. Then I send a bill.
Bruce looks at the wall map. Pins and threads trace a path from the tower to the harbour to the old mills, and he follows it with a finger.
If this works, I will have a man who can tell me where the whole thing begins.
Then I have a man who can tell me nothing, and a crane that does not belong to anybody.
A very fine ending for a very fine evening.
Fox sets his cup down. For a moment the three of them stand there in the lamp light, none of them quite ready to say what they are doing.
A low rumble from the hill above: a goods train, miles off, carrying the ordinary night to somewhere else.
Bruce rolls his sleeves another turn. Alfred straightens the tray by half an inch. Fox looks at the cake as if it might be armed.
Eat the cake, Mr Wayne. It is the last easy thing you will do all month.
A tower of glass by the sea. A high atrium bright as a refrigerator, a reception desk shaped like a ship, lifts opening on to nothing. Staff move across the marble in neat lines.
BRUCE WAYNE crosses it at an unhurried pace with FOX's introduction in his hand. Two of Lau's aides come to meet him, smiling in unison.
Mr Wayne. We are honoured. Mr Lau is expecting you.
They take him up a glass lift. The city shrinks below. At the top, a wide office with a desk and a window running floor to ceiling.
LAU rises from behind the desk. Small, neat, a man who takes up exactly as much space as he needs and not a centimetre more.
A pleasure. Forgive the view. People say it is a distraction. I find it keeps the customers honest.
I would like to understand the terms of your work.
Naturally. May I offer you tea?
And a short history of a modest firm?
It is always short. We take what clients bring us. We keep it where it is safe. We do not ask where it was before.
An old one. The word is discretion. Most of our clients are very respectable people with very respectable problems.
Bruce sits. A tea tray arrives. Through the window, a pair of gulls rise and tilt along the face of the tower.
And in the case of an investigation?
We are across a sea. And a very long way from anyone who would want to ask.
What about the men who need reassurance?
I give it. I give it by telephone, and by video, and when needed by the occasional afternoon.
Yes. Mr Wayne, you are a careful man yourself, I think. I do not need to tell you that careful men leave very few reasons to be visited.
Bruce lifts the cup. He is looking past Lau at a door in the corner of the room, a plain one painted to match the wall.
It is the one I use at night.
There is a gentleman in the other time zone who will not be told it is morning.
He smiles. The tea is very good. Bruce finishes it, stands, and offers a hand.
I will be in touch about a deposit.
Please do. A little earlier next time and I will be here to meet you.
In the lift going down, Bruce looks up once at the roof of the cab, at the quiet small hatch in the ceiling. Then at the numbers falling.
The doors open on the atrium. Staff cross the marble in their neat lines, and nobody looks at him twice. It is, he thinks, the best thing a building can say about itself.
At the revolving door he pauses to let a courier pass, and takes one last, easy look at the guard on the east stairs, the second guard at the lift, the camera above the desk.
Night. The tower from below, black glass and a hundred lit windows. A very tall crane stands in the empty plot next door, a red lamp winking at its tip.
On the roof of the tower, a gate bangs. LAU'S GUARDS cross the rooftop in pairs, torches sweeping. One stops at the lift housing, looks up at the crane, shrugs.

A shape moves in the lee of the water tanks. BATMAN, in a darker suit than before, unwinds a coil of grey cable from the black box. He clips it to a point on his belt and tests it twice against the parapet.
In the office below, the door in the corner opens. Lau steps out in shirtsleeves and sits at a long desk with a laptop and a phone. He does not look up.
Batman lowers himself over the edge on the cable, slow and quiet, spiders his way along the glass until he is outside the night office. He taps the pane once.
Lau looks up. The window is empty. He frowns and returns to his screen. Another tap, from a different corner.
The window explodes inward in a hail of small glass. Batman swings through it in a single movement, takes Lau by the collar and lifts him out of the chair.
There are guards. There are four guards. They are all very well paid.
Please. I will give you anything. I have a great deal of money.
Batman hooks a second line to Lau's belt and wraps an arm around his chest. A door bursts open; two guards with torches and pistols.
Batman drops to the window, steps off the sill into the dark with Lau against him. The guards fire; glass sings off the frames.
A beat of weightless silence. Then the cable snaps taut and the two of them are dragged upward through the night as the crane takes the load.
The city drops away beneath their boots. Tail lights crawl along the ring road like a necklace someone has dropped, and the sea beyond the port is a long black sheet.
Lau has shut his eyes tight. His spectacles swing from a cord at his neck and tap against Batman's chest with every sway of the line.
The wind drives at them sideways. Batman turns his back into it and keeps one arm steady around the little accountant, who is saying something in a language the wind takes away.
The guards run to the broken window. Below the sill, the air is empty.
They look. High above, against the stars, two dark figures dwindle toward the crane's red lamp.
One of them fires a pistol upward, twice, uselessly. The shots go off into the dark and nothing answers them.
In the street below, a taxi driver has stopped to watch. He lifts his phone to take a picture and the screen shows only a bright smear of red lamp against black.
On the crane's jib, a tiny cab. Inside it, a crouching figure in work overalls who has been waiting for two hours.
At the tip of the jib the line goes slack and Batman steps on to the metal frame with Lau under one arm. Behind them, the tower's lights flick on window by window, searching.
Batman hauls Lau down the length of the jib, one handhold at a time. At the base a car is waiting, engine running, rear door open.
He tosses Lau in the back, jumps in after. The car pulls out before the door is closed.
Sirens, far off and late. On the tower roof, the guards are lighting a flare to see where they went.
INT. INTERROGATION ROOM, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT
A bare room with a steel table and two chairs. A single tube light hums over it. On the other side of a two-way mirror, GORDON and HARVEY DENT watch.
LAU sits in the middle of the room in torn overalls, a plastic cup of water in front of him. He is shaking, and trying very hard to stop.
He is a witness. He has asked for protection.
From everybody. He says the people he works for will kill him.
He knows. That is why he is being polite to us.
Dent opens the door and goes in. He sits on the other side of the table. He puts a notepad between them.
Mr Lau. I am Harvey Dent. I am from the District Attorney's office.
I have been told. I have also been told you are very good in court.
A man who carried me out of a window.
Dent glances at the mirror, then back.
Mr Lau, there are three things I want from you. The first is the names on the accounts.
There are no names. There are numbers.
Then the numbers. The second is the route the money takes between the vans and the sea.
That is longer. I would need paper and a very big table.
We have those. The third is a name. The man who gave the order for a bank to be robbed in Mylapore.
Lau's cup rattles on the steel.
That was not one of my clients.
I do not know. A man arrived at a meeting once, uninvited. He asked for a seat. He was not on any list.
I cannot. It was a bad line. A smile, a coat. Something about the voice. When he left, nobody could say what he had wanted.
He wanted the others to be afraid of him instead of me. It worked beautifully.
Dent writes a note, tears it off and slides it under his own wrist.
You will give us everything. All of it, in writing, with dates.
A room with a lock on the inside and the best lawyer in the country on your side of the table.
I am only the best lawyer in the city. The country is very big.
Lau lets out a thin laugh. He picks up the pen Dent has left and for the first time begins to write.
Through the mirror, Gordon turns to a younger officer behind him.
Get this man a decent chair and some food that has not been through a machine.
The mill again, the same trestle table and the same eight men. The laptop is closed. The mood is thick, nervous, short on cigar smoke and long on silence.
A man from a glass tower is in a police station. Our records are in his head. Somebody tell me what this means.
At the far end of the mill, a door opens. A thin figure comes in, unhurried, dragging a canvas bag.
He wears a long purple coat with the collar turned up. His face is painted white, with a smear of red where the mouth should be and a pair of black circles round the eyes.
He walks to the table. Every man in the room has a hand under his coat or his jacket.
You are in the wrong building.
I am in the right one. Only everyone else is in the wrong building.
He heaves the canvas bag on to the table. It lands with a soft heavy thud.
Nobody moves. The Joker flips open the bag. Bundles of used notes, tied in rubber bands, each with a small purple sticker in the shape of a grin.
It is the Mylapore bank. Or most of it. I have kept a little for the electricity.
You robbed the bank we were using.
I robbed the bank you were using. And I killed everyone who helped me, which is a very honest way to run a business.
A person with a proposal. I would like to take the thing that is bothering you off your hands.
Your friend in the cape. The one who comes in through the ceiling.
A long look. The Broker takes off his spectacles and wipes them with his sleeve.
He is a problem for the police.
The police have had him for a year and a half. And have they got him?
Of whatever you were going to give a man to do the job. Half now, half when it is finished.
You are asking us to pay a clown.
I am asking you to pay a specialist. It is only a matter of the paint.
He leans across the table and takes a stack of notes from the bag. He splits it neatly with his thumb and pushes half back across the table.
That half is yours. I only want the other half to arrive in the morning, in a bag exactly like this one.
The Joker straightens. He looks round the mill, at the high windows and the rusting machines and the faces of the men.
You have no better offers. You have one bank down and an accountant in a police station. And I have one thing you do not.
No reason to be anywhere else.
Silence. Then Gambol, whose chin still has a bandage on it, steps forward.
I do not trust him. I say we put him in a drum.
I would like to see you try. Only I would ask that you do it after you have read the card.
He takes a purple card from his sleeve. He sets it on top of the notes, face up, and walks out of the mill with his hands in his pockets.
Maroni looks at the card for a long time. Then he picks it up and puts it in his pocket.
INT. BRUCE'S PENTHOUSE, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT
A wide penthouse at night. Floor-to-ceiling glass, the city laid out underneath like a map of a larger and more tolerant country.
BRUCE WAYNE stands at the window in a dressing gown. ALFRED comes in with a tray and sets it on a low table.
I thought you might need something to wash the evening away.
Then you are the first person I have heard describe a night in that suit as good.
Bruce takes the cup. He looks at the city, at the small lights drifting on the water.
I think I can see an end to it, Alfred.
All of this. If Harvey does what he says he can do, there will be no need for me. The mob will be gone, the courts will work, and nobody will need a man in the sky.
And you will do what then?
I will be a person with a company and a lot of years.
I have always thought that would suit you.
It would. It would suit me very well.
Alfred pours his own tea and takes the chair by the window.
She seemed pleased with the new prosecutor.
I think he is a good man. I think he might be a better one than I could ever be.
A man who does not hide in the dark is a different sort of good.
That is exactly what I mean.
Alfred does not answer for a moment. He stirs the tea slowly, watching the leaves go round.
In my experience, sir, the city does not retire the people who save it. It forgets them. That is a great deal more comfortable than a medal.
Is that what you want for me?
I want you to be warm, fed, and not on fire. I think that is the most any manservant can want.
Bruce laughs, short and tired. He sits on the arm of a sofa.
And if somebody else is wearing the suit?
Then he will be somebody I have never made lemon cake for. A very sad thing.
I am here to be. Drink your tea.
Bruce drinks. Behind him, on the glass, the city lights tremble faintly in a small gust of wind. He does not notice. Alfred does.

Alfred rises, takes the empty cup, and stands a moment looking out. A long way down, a single patrol car edges along the quay with its blue light turning, and he follows it until it goes behind a warehouse.
Police headquarters at night. The same long room, half the lights off, a single fan turning above the map. GORDON and RAMIREZ stand over a desk with a plain white envelope between them.
THE COMMISSIONER comes in at a brisk walk, a fat man in a crumpled uniform, THE MAYOR a half step behind him, a lean man with a hurry in his hands.
A letter. It was brought to the front desk about an hour ago by a boy who said a man gave him fifty rupees.
Gordon unfolds the page. He reads it aloud, flat and quiet.

"To the leaders of the city. A masked man puts you to sleep. I shall wake you. Each night a person on this list will go. I will start with the least important and work upward. The list is attached. Please do not reply. I will know when you have received it."
He puts the page down. The mayor sits heavily on the corner of a desk.
It came with a hand. The boy had a bag. There was a hand in it.
This is the same person who robbed the bank.
The card is the same. The hand is not on anyone's list, which I take to mean it is the most important thing in the envelope.
Gordon unfolds the second sheet. Five names, handwritten in purple ink. A judge. A police officer. A journalist. The Commissioner. The Mayor.
Then I do not understand the order. The bottom should be the least important.
Perhaps he thinks the least important man is the one who makes the speeches.
This is not the time for comedy, Gordon.
No, sir. It is a time for protection. I would like three men on every name.
Where do I find three men?
From the banks. We have constables sitting on empty vaults in thirty places.
He is not our concern. This is a man with a pen and a very short fuse.
Yes, sir. I will need the whole force and some luck.
He goes out. The mayor lingers by the map, running a finger down the list, stopping at his own name and then at the Commissioner's.
Go home. Lock the door. And do not make any speeches.
Then perhaps this is the time to start being less important.
The ballroom of the heritage hotel. Chandeliers, polished marble, a wide stage with a banner: DENT FOR THE CITY. A hundred and twenty guests in evening wear, four waiters to every table.
BRUCE WAYNE stands near the stage in a dinner jacket, a glass of lime soda in his hand and a smile on his face that does not touch his eyes.
HARVEY DENT comes through the crowd, shaking hands as he goes. RACHEL walks at his shoulder, a half-pace behind, scanning the room.
You look more cheerful than a man hosting a party should.
It is a very large party. I have not had to speak to anyone for ten minutes.
He has been standing under the chandelier so nobody can find him.
It is the best place in the room. All the light is above it.
THE COMMISSIONER and THE MAYOR arrive together, each with a bodyguard at his elbow. The mayor takes the stage, taps the microphone, and clears his throat.
Friends. I have been asked to say a few words, and I will say very few.
Polite laughter. He glances once at the doors, then back at the crowd.
Our city has been through a difficult year. We have been told that nobody can fix it. I am here to say that Harvey Dent will.
Applause. Dent steps up to the microphone, takes it off the stand and holds it very lightly.
Thank you. I will not give a speech. I only wish to say one thing. For a long time we have been told the people who run this city are not the ones in the town hall.
He pauses. He lets the room come in close.
I would like to say tonight that we are taking it back. Not with a mask. In a court, in daylight, where everybody can see.
A roar. Bruce applauds along with the rest, and Rachel stops watching the room and watches him.
You are not much of a liar.
You are the worst. It is why I like you.

A waiter passes with a tray of glasses. Bruce steadies one with a finger and, at the same moment, notices the man behind the waiter. Heavy, grey-faced, a cap pulled down. He is not carrying a tray and he is not looking at the stage.
The man meets his eye. He smiles briefly, and slides back into the crowd.
Nothing. It is a very long evening. I am going to have a word with the manager.
He weaves between the tables. At the back of the ballroom, a service door closes softly. The hall is full of laughter and the band has begun to play.
INT. BRUCE'S PENTHOUSE, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT
The penthouse after the party. A smaller gathering: thirty guests in silks and jackets, the lamps low, Bruce's apartment turned into a lounge. Rain on the glass.
HARVEY DENT and RACHEL stand by the window with glasses. BRUCE WAYNE comes out of the corridor, glancing over his shoulder.
A noise at the door. The guests turn. The lift opens and eight men come out, each in a clown mask, each carrying something under a coat.
The party freezes. Someone's glass hits the floor and breaks. In the middle of the eight, a ninth man, in purple, his face painted, walks forward like a host.
Good evening, everyone. Please remain exactly where you are. If you can do that, nobody will need to be hurt.
A guest, an older man, steps forward with his hands up.
Only to look. I am considering a long stay in this city. I wanted to meet the people who might be unhappy about it.
He moves among the guests, studying faces like a buyer in a market. He stops in front of Dent.
You. You are the one with the coin.
Of course. The man who is going to save everyone. How do you say it? Without a mask?
In daylight. It is a very nice line. I think I will use it.
Dent steps in front of Rachel. The Joker looks at him, amused, then past him.
She is not part of this.
Then why are you standing in front of her?
Bruce moves slowly to the side, unnoticed, until he is standing behind a stone pillar. The Joker is circling again.
Tell me. If I were to be a very bad man tonight, who would you want to be standing in front of you?
Nobody. I stand in front of myself.
A brave answer. And a very dangerous one.
He pulls a thin blade from his sleeve. In the same moment Bruce steps out from behind the pillar, in the middle of the room, a drunk and foolish host.
There you are. I wondered whether the entertainment would arrive. Do you take requests?
The Joker's head turns. The blade pauses.
Another one with something to say.
I only wondered about the fee. I am very bad at party budgets.
Do you know, I do not think you are who you are pretending to be.
In the half-second the Joker takes to consider it, Bruce hurls a champagne tray across the lounge. It strikes two masked men and the room explodes.
Guests scatter. Dent drags Rachel behind a sofa. The henchmen shout, fire a shot into the ceiling, a chandelier shivers.
The Joker catches Rachel by the arm as she runs, hauls her to the open terrace doors. Rain blows in on the marble floor.
Come and look at the city. It is such a good one.
He pushes her backward through the doors. Rachel's heels slide on the wet stone. She goes over the low balustrade.
Bruce does not stop. He goes through the doors at a sprint, past the Joker, and over the edge in a flat dive, dressing gown flying.
The rain, and the lights below. Rachel falls, spinning, and Bruce falls after her, faster, arms out.
He catches her at the third floor, twists, takes the impact on his back through the awning of a restaurant. Canvas tears. They land together on the pavement, in a heap of striped cloth.
Rachel gasps. Bruce lies on his back, breathing, looking up at the terrace far above, where a small purple figure leans over and waves.
I am very good at running.
She looks at him in the wet street light. Something large is moving behind her eyes.
EXT. MOUNT ROAD FUNERAL ROUTE - DAY
Mount Road in daylight, closed to traffic for a mile. Mourners lined along both pavements, hundreds deep, in white. Overhead, a thin high cloud.
A funeral wagon rolls slowly down the centre of the road, drawn by two black horses and flanked by police on motorcycles. A band plays something low and sorrowful.
On the wagon, under a mountain of wreaths, lies a coffin draped in the police flag. THE COMMISSIONER is at rest.
Behind it walk GORDON and HARVEY DENT, side by side, in dress uniform and black suit. A pace behind them walks THE MAYOR with a guard at each elbow.
He is out there. I can feel it.
There are four hundred men on the rooftops.
Gordon's eyes go up. Rooftops, water tanks, a ragged row of television aerials. A small glint, very high up, which could be glass.
He grabs a constable by the sleeve and points. The constable runs.
Among the marching police in the front rows, one man in a dress cap breaks formation. He raises a rifle that was hidden down the leg of his trousers.
The band plays. The Mayor, unaware, steps forward to lay a wreath on the wagon.
Behind the wagon, the marching rows pass in perfect step, white gloves swinging, boots striking the road together. A drummer's stick rises and falls like a slow heartbeat.
From the crowd, small things are being handed up: a child's drawing, a bunch of marigolds, a folded newspaper with the dead man's photograph.
He throws himself at the mayor. A single shot from the rooftop cracks over the music. Gordon and the mayor fall together between two flower-laden wagons.
Dent pulls his own pistol from under his jacket and fires at the man in the dress cap. The man crumples. The mourners panic, run in every direction.
On the rooftop, the glint disappears.
Gordon lies on the road, one arm across the mayor. A dark patch spreads along his sleeve. The mayor stares at him, mouth open.
He is hit. He is hit.
Dent drops beside them. He feels at Gordon's neck, then tears the sleeve open, and his face loosens with relief.
Shoulder. It missed everything that matters.
Then why does it feel like it took the lot?
A constable's whistle. Four police run to carry Gordon, grey and swearing, toward an ambulance. The crowd falls silent around them.
At the back of the crowd, in an old overcoat with the collar high, a small dignified man named ALFRED has taken off his hat. He is not looking at the wounded. He is looking at the sky.
On a distant roof, a figure in black stands against the clouds, watching the ambulance go. Then he too is gone.
The Sessions Court, in a hush. The room is packed, but nobody is speaking. HARVEY DENT stands at the prosecutor's table, with RACHEL beside him. THE JUDGE sits high on the bench, quiet.
A small crowd of reporters sits at the back with notebooks open. A boy outside holds up a newspaper with a headline: THE POLICE ARE PAYING.
Mr Dent. You asked for the court's time.
Yes, my lord. I would like to make a statement.
Concerning the man whom everybody in this city is looking for.
A stir through the gallery. Rachel turns, alarmed.
I am about to end it.
He steps out from behind the table and walks to the middle of the floor. A hundred faces follow him.
For days, a man has told us that a person each night will die until the one in the mask gives himself up. A good man died yesterday. A judge on Monday. These are our people.
My lord, I know the rules. I am not asking the court to bend them. I am asking the court to hear that I have committed an offence.
I am the one who has been wearing the mask.
The court erupts. Reporters shove forward. The Judge pounds the bench and a clerk drops a stack of files. Rachel stares at Dent.
I will accept whatever the law requires. I only ask that you take me now. And that you tell the man who is killing people that he has what he asked for.
The Judge looks at him for a long time. The room settles slowly, like dust.
Mr Dent, I will not rule on a confession I do not believe.
That is for you to decide, my lord.
It is not for me alone. But it will be for somebody. Bailiff.
A bailiff steps forward. Dent holds out his wrists and a constable puts on the cuffs, very slightly too tight.
Rachel catches his sleeve as he is led past.
You are not a liar either. Why are you doing this?
He is walked out of the courtroom. The reporters crowd behind him, flashes popping like a small firework display.
INT. BRUCE'S PENTHOUSE, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT
The penthouse, a late hour. One lamp lit. BRUCE WAYNE sits in an armchair in shirtsleeves, staring at the city. ALFRED stands near the door with a folded sheet of paper.
RACHEL is at the window with her back to them. She has not changed out of the dress she wore to court.
I wrote you a letter. I was going to give it to you tonight.
I changed my mind. I am giving it to Alfred. I want him to keep it.
I am a very good place to keep things.
He is the only man you have not been able to lie to.
She turns. She walks across the room and hands the envelope to Alfred, who tucks it into his waistcoat without looking.
When it is over, when you are tired of all this, you can read it.
It says what I could never manage to say while you were wearing it.
He stands. They look at each other. The lamp ticks as it cools.
Harvey took everybody's place. It was the best thing I have ever seen and the stupidest.
He will not last a night in a cell.
Then you know what to do.
I have never been very good at doing what I should.
You have always been very good at doing what you must.
She moves toward the door. Alfred holds it open with a small bow.
And Bruce. Whatever you do tomorrow, do it for the person you are. Not the one you play.
I do not always know which that is.
I think you do. You are just afraid it will be too ordinary.
She leaves. The door closes. Bruce stands for a long time, then crosses to a small table and pours himself a glass of water.
You are going to hand yourself in.
Tomorrow morning. In front of everyone.
He will stop when he has what he wants.
I have never found that to be true of anyone. Least of all a man who paints his face.
Bruce sets the glass down. For a moment he is utterly still, looking at his own reflection in the black window.
Then it is a good thing I will not be the one to find out.

Night. A long elevated expressway curving above the city, empty except for a convoy: two armoured vans, front and rear, and between them a third, with a barred rear window. Eight police cars flank them.

In the middle van, HARVEY DENT sits in cuffs on a steel bench. He looks calm, even bored. GORDON, alive and unshaven under a cap he has borrowed, rides in the passenger seat of the lead car, with a radio in his lap.
Everyone keep your spacing. If anything comes down the road, do not stop for it. We take the long way to the station and that is all.
The radio crackles. A low drone rises under the engine noise. In the mirror, headlights approach fast from behind, far too tall and far too wide.
Something is coming up the road. A lorry. Very big.

The lorry hits the rear van with a boom. Metal shrieks. The rear van skids across two lanes and into the barrier; the lorry shoves it off the road and over the edge of the flyover, where it falls out of sight.
The convoy accelerates. Behind it, the lorry climbs out of its own smoke and keeps coming.
On the lorry's roof, a figure in purple stands with his coat flying, a long tube on his shoulder. He grins like a child at a fair.
The wind drags the coat out behind him like a flag. Cars in the opposite lane brake, swerve, and scatter on to the shoulder as the convoy thunders by.
The second armoured van drifts out to guard the middle one's flank. Its driver glances in the mirror and goes pale at what is filling it.
The first rocket takes out the nearest police car, which vanishes in a ball of orange fire. A second car swerves through the flames and rolls.
Debris rains across the roadway. A wheel bounces down the lane ahead and clears the barrier in a long lazy arc.
Gordon's driver keeps his foot flat and his eyes on the road. In the back seat, a constable crosses himself with a pistol still in his hand.
In the middle van, Dent braces himself on the bench. The guard opposite him curses and pulls his pistol.
Keep your head down, sir. He is not going to reach us.
A third rocket. The lead van takes it. It jackknifes across the road, slides sideways and stops, burning. The convoy splits around it.
The surviving police cars scatter between the burning shell and the barrier, tyres howling. One clips the van's flank and spins, skating on its roof for fifty yards before it stops.
Sirens, shouted orders, a radio crackling with names. Nobody in it can hear anybody else.
From an exit ramp, with a thrum like a thundercloud, a black bike climbs on to the road. Batman, low over the handlebars, hands steady, weaving between burning wrecks.
I have no left lane left.
He passes the middle van and tips the bike on its side, sliding it under the front of the lorry in a spray of sparks. The lorry's cab lurches; the driver wrestles the wheel.
The Joker on the roof drops to a crouch, grabs the cab for balance, and fires once more at the middle van, point-blank.
The rocket never leaves the tube. Batman's bike has flipped up on its rear wheel, and the Joker's tube is wrenched out of his hands and spins away over the barrier.
The lorry slews wildly. Its trailer sweeps the barrier and tears out a long section of the railing. Cars behind it pile up in a crumple of horns and glass.
The trailer's back doors fly open and a river of cardboard boxes spills across the road, bursting into a snow of printed purple cards that whirls up in the headlamps.
Batman's bike skids through them, wheel slick, and rights itself against all odds.
Gordon steps out of his own car, pistol in hand, and walks into the smoke.
Put your hands where I can see them.
The Joker, standing on the cab of the lorry, spreads his arms wide.
Batman's bike roars past Gordon and straight at the lorry. The Joker raises a pistol, sees the headlamp swell, and leaps down.
EXT. PORT TUNNEL APPROACH, ISLAND GROUNDS - NIGHT

The mouth of an old port tunnel, a half-mile of curved concrete under the harbour approach. Floodlights and wreckage. The lorry has come to rest against the tunnel wall, its cab crushed, its trailer open like a ripped can.
Police cars arrive in twos and threes, doors flung wide. Constables pour out. They stop at the edge of the light.
Dust still hangs in the floodlights. Somewhere inside the tunnel a bolt of tin falls from the roof and clangs for a long time.
A medic crouches beside the lorry's crushed cab. He looks in, stands, and shakes his head at the nearest constable: nobody inside.
The Joker walks out of the tunnel mouth into the glare. His coat is torn at one shoulder. He is smiling, and bleeding a little from the lip.
I surrender. I think I will surrender. Is that how it is said?
Nobody moves. A ring of pistols come up around him. Gordon strides forward through them, his cap gone, his face black with soot.
Gladly. I have been on them all week.
He kneels slowly, laces his fingers behind his head. A constable steps in and cuffs him, hard.
You do not have to be rough. I came a very long way to be here.
You have a great deal to answer for.
I do. But I think you want to ask the questions first. I would, if I were you.
Gordon grabs him by the front of his coat and drags him upright. For a moment they are very close. The Joker's smile widens.
Is he coming? The man who hurt his hands on my lorry?
I do not know who you mean.
On the road behind them, a black bike lies on its side, its engine ticking, a thin wisp of smoke from the exhaust. There is no rider.
High on the tunnel's wall, behind the floodlights, a shadow detaches itself and moves a little closer.
Gordon turns away. His men march the Joker toward a police van. The clown lifts his head and looks straight up, to where the shadow is.
He does not wave. He nods, once, like a man at a railway station seeing a friend arrive on a delayed train.
The van doors close on him. Through the little barred window, the painted smile can be seen for as long as it is in the light.
Gordon watches the van's tail lamps shrink in the tunnel mouth. Then he looks up to the wall, where the shadow has already gone.
INT. INTERROGATION ROOM, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT

The interrogation room. Steel table, steel chairs, a wall clock stopped at ten past three. The Joker sits on one side of the table, cuffed to a ring, his coat hanging off the back of the chair. Behind the mirror, GORDON watches with RAMIREZ.
BATMAN is not in the room. Then he is. A very slight sound, a breath of air from the vent, and he is standing in the corner as if he had been there all night.
Hello. I was beginning to think you were not coming.
Batman crosses the room. He does not sit. He lays both hands flat on the table and leans in.
I know many things. I know that the clock on that wall has stopped at ten past three. Somebody in this building likes the idea of it always being that time.
Harvey Dent and Rachel Dawes. Where are they?
They are in two places. That is the good part.
Oh, I will. Only you must try to be patient. I have been very patient with you.
Batman straightens. He walks around the table, slowly. The Joker's eyes follow him without moving his head.
You do not like me, I think. I do not mind. It is very rare for someone to take me so seriously.
You have taken a great many lives.
A great many people. Some of them I only borrowed.
That is not a question for a man in your position. You have a place in this city, but I have a use for it. Do you know the difference?
A place is where you are put. A use is what you are good for.
And what are you good for?
Asking people what they are good for.

He laughs, a small dry cough of a laugh that goes on a little too long. Batman takes the chair on the other side of the table and turns it around. He sits, finally, with his arms across the back of it.
Two. One for each person you would like to save. And a very, very small amount of time.
Batman does not. He keeps his eyes on the painted face.
It is stopped. Do you see? It is always ten past three. I have to say, Batman, I do not believe you are very good at being told when time is running out.
You have a choice to make.
You can tell me where they are, or you can tell the doctor why your jaw does not close.
The Joker tilts his head. He seems to consider it genuinely, with real interest.
You are going to hurt me.
Go on, then. I would like to see what is under the cowl.
Batman rises. He rounds the table, takes the Joker by the collar, and slams him against the wall. The cuffs rattle on the ring.
Harder. You are not even trying.
Batman hits him. The Joker's head snaps sideways. He laughs. He keeps laughing, with blood on his teeth.
There it is. I knew there was a man in there. A very serious man.
You can only save one. Do you know what that means? It means you must choose. And for a person who keeps everyone safe, that is the worst thing in the world.
Behind the mirror, Gordon pounds a fist on the glass.
Batman does not hear him. He is looking at the Joker's smeared grin, his own gloved hand, the red on the knuckles.
Here is what I will do. I will give you two addresses. A mill and a depot. One has her. One has him. And you may go to either, but not both.
I am the one man here who never does. It is my only good quality.
He gives the addresses in a sing-song. Batman releases him. He turns and strides to the door.
Hurry. The traffic is bad at this hour.
Batman is gone. In the mirror, Gordon stares at his own reflection. In the chair, the Joker smiles at the clock that has stopped.
A minute passes. Then two. Ramirez comes in from the corridor with a tin cup of tea and stops, uncertain, at the other side of the glass.
The Joker begins to hum, tunelessly, a few bars of an old film song, and taps out the rhythm on the table with one cuffed hand.
Gordon takes the cup from Ramirez, stares into it, and puts it down untouched.

A cold room in the old mill, one bare bulb. RACHEL sits on an oil drum with her wrists bound behind her. A rope runs from her ankles to the drum's rim. A small box with a flashing red light is taped to her ribs.
A JOKER HENCHMAN, in a clown mask and working overalls, props a mobile phone on a crate in front of her and thumbs a button.
The phone buzzes. A voice, tinny and distant.
Somewhere I cannot see. A chair, a wall. I think there are drums. I think I am in a depot.
He has put the two of us in different places.
He has. Is there someone with you?
One man. He is not saying much.
The henchman folds his arms and leans on the wall. A timer on the box beside her begins to count down from three hundred.
Rachel, listen. I am going to get out of this chair. I have a pin in my pocket. I can open the cuffs.
Because you are not going to get here in time.
Silence on the line. The timer drops to two hundred and ninety.
I wrote a letter to Bruce.
I did not tell you what was in it.
I told him I could not wait for him. I told him I was going to marry you.
A long breath on the line.
You did not say yes to me.
The timer is at two hundred. The henchman watches it without expression.
Then do not be afraid. I am coming.
The call crackles. The line goes thin. The timer ticks. At one hundred, the bare bulb above her flickers once, twice, and steadies.
Rachel sits very straight on the drum. She looks at the red light on her ribs, and then at the phone, and then at the dim empty door.
A drip of water from a broken gutter lands on the concrete near her foot. She counts three drops and then forces herself to stop counting.
The red light blinks. The timer is a clean white number against a black field, and it does not hurry and does not wait.
Outside, very far off, the first engine of a bike. It does not stop.

An empty office in the depot. Bare walls, a high barred window, three oil drums in a corner. HARVEY DENT sits in a chair bolted to the floor, his wrists tied to the arms. A phone on the floor in front of him shows a call in progress.
A JOKER HENCHMAN stands in the doorway. He is bored, and chewing something.
No answer. The call counter reads 04:30, then 04:31.
She has gone quiet. It is the usual thing.
What have you done to her?
Nothing. It is what he has done. I only keep the line.
Dent twists his wrists against the rope. A thin line of blood appears under the knot. He holds his breath and works at it.
Outside the window, the evening light is going copper. A bike's engine, a long way off.
And you are a lawyer. I think that is worse.
He laughs, then stops. The bike's engine has become a roar. The window glass trembles.
The henchman steps back into the doorway, pulling a pistol from his belt. A dark shape comes through the window frame and takes him from behind. The pistol clatters across the floor.
Batman drops the man like a sack of grain and rushes to Dent. He tears at the ropes.
Where have you been? She is dying.
I came as soon as I could.
The mill. In Ambattur. I was told this is where you were.
No. No. He told you the wrong one. He has put us in the wrong places.
Think. He wants you to choose.
Batman's hand stops on the rope.
Both men look at the phone on the floor. The call timer reads 04:59. It reads 05:00. It stops.
A silence like a held note. And then, very faint through the speaker, a deep soft thud that shakes the table and takes the line away.
Dent stares at the phone. He does not breathe. Batman puts a hand on his shoulder.
He says the name twice, three times, the third as if it were the only word left. A crash behind them: the drums in the corner have begun to hiss.
She has gone. I did not even hear the end of the sentence.
The hiss rises. Fire licks along a pipe.
The depot, from outside. A flash from the office window, a roar, and then a sheet of white flame climbing the side of the building. The drums catch one by one.
Smoke boils up past the gantry. A fire tender is racing along the access road, bell clanging, but it is a minute away and every second is a long time.
In the yard, half in the blaze, Batman drags HARVEY DENT out through the burning doorway. He is carrying him over his shoulders, cape smouldering, the side of Dent's face already black.
Hold on. I have you. Hold on.
A drum behind them goes up. Flame rolls across the yard. Batman throws himself flat, covering Dent with his own body as the wave passes over.
It passes. The yard is a field of fire. In the dark of Batman's shoulder, a thin scream.
Dent has turned his head. One half of his face is whole. The other half is a map of raw red and white.
I can feel it. I can feel it, all of it.
She is gone. She is gone and I am here.
You said you would reach her.
No. Of course you did not.
The fire tender screams into the yard. Firemen pour out. A stretcher, a hose, a brusque medic. Batman lowers Dent on to the stretcher and steps back.
The medic cuts the burned shirt open. The firemen do not look at Dent's face for very long.
Dent's good hand shoots out and grips his arm. His eyes, red-rimmed, are very steady.
I made the only one I could.
Then you are a fool. And I am the proof.
His hand falls away. The stretcher moves. Batman watches until the doors close, then looks at the burning depot behind him. The flames are green and gold and they do not go out.

A government hospital in Royapettah, a corridor of green walls and old ceiling fans. A long ward in the burns unit: ten beds, two nurses, a pair of overhead lamps that flicker when the generator coughs.
HARVEY DENT lies in the last bed, bandaged on the left side from forehead to jaw, one eye swollen shut. A drip runs into his arm. He is awake, staring at the ceiling.
A NURSE comes through the door with a tray, checks his chart and the drip.
You should be resting, sir. Nothing helps like sleep.
I have not been able to.
No. I need to feel it.
She nods, uncertain, and writes on the chart. When she goes out, the ward is quiet except for a monitor beeping down the row.
A man in an orderly's white coat comes in with a mop. He keeps his head down, working along the floor, until he reaches the foot of Dent's bed.
Dent turns his head. The orderly lifts his, just enough. Beneath a nurse's cap, a painted face, with a scar of red at the mouth.
Me. I came to say I was sorry for your loss.
In a moment. I would only like to look.
He pulls a chair up to the bed and sits, mop across his knees. He studies the bandaged face.
It is a fine piece of work. Was there a surgeon?
They would not take the bandage off.
Then I will tell you what is under it. A man who is half what he was. And half what he could be.
Please what? You do not want to hear the diagnosis?
Dent turns away. The Joker leans in, as gentle as a nurse.

Let me tell you something. I did not take her from you. The people you trusted did. The ones who were meant to have lined the road with guards. The policemen who were supposed to know where the van was going.
Your friend. The one who runs about on the roofs. He said he would keep you safe. And the Commissioner. And your very polite friends in the force.
He takes a slow breath, almost tender.
They all made promises. And everyone I have ever met who made a promise ended up breaking it.
Only for you to stop expecting them to keep their word. It is quite freeing.
He slides a small bottle of pills across the sheet. Dent does not look at it. The Joker takes out a flat tin of paint and dabs a small mark on the back of Dent's hand.
A little souvenir. In case you have to remember.
He stands, takes up the mop. At the door he stops, looks back, and his voice is quite kind.
Look around. It is the same ward. Same lamp. Same people. The only thing that has changed is what you know.
He goes out. The monitor goes on beeping. Dent lies still. In the dark of his good eye, something has moved, very slightly, a long way down.

A night street outside the hospital. A crowd of evacuees stands behind a barrier: nurses in white, patients in gowns, relatives in raincoats, all looking up at the long dark face of the hospital wing.
The police have the road closed. Ambulances line the kerb, back doors wide. A hospital bus waits at the gate, engine running.
GORDON stands at the barrier, a loudhailer in his hand and a cold cup of tea in the other. He is hoarse and sleepless.
Everybody keep moving. Please walk, do not run. There is room in the buses for all of you.
A hundred and twenty people shuffle past, eyes on the ground. A boy leads an old man with a drip stand. A nurse carries a baby in a blanket.
A porter pushes an empty wheelchair that squeaks on every turn. A surgeon in a stained gown walks backwards, counting heads under his breath.
Behind them the hospital's windows glow yellow, floor on floor. In one of them, a curtain stirs, though nobody is meant to be inside.
Among them, in a nurse's cap and a long coat, walks a small figure with a carefully bored expression. He looks up and down the line of patients as if choosing a seat in a cinema.
Gordon sees him. He sees the cap, then the hands, then the thing on the cap's brim, a purple sticker with a grin.
Two constables turn, startled. The figure in the cap stops, lifts one gloved finger and then a small black device from his pocket.
The finger presses. For a half-second nothing happens. Then, across the face of the hospital wing, a hundred windows bloom in white light.
The explosion rolls over the street. The crowd falls flat. Glass rains on the barriers. A column of black smoke climbs from the roof, and slowly, with a groan, the wing begins to fold in on itself.
Gordon is on his knees in the road. Constables scramble back to their feet. Behind him the buses are all still standing, all still full, and not one passenger is hurt.
The wing sinks, floor on floor, in a cloud of dust. When it clears, the sky is red from below.
Fire engines surge forward. Firemen lay hoses across the debris, helmets glinting. A hundred voices call out names in the dark.
A child cries somewhere in the dust, and a policeman, running, is already answering it.
In the dust, in the roadway, a nurse's cap lies upside down. A purple sticker, a card, a small mirror.
Gordon picks up the card. He reads it. He folds it in half and puts it in his pocket.
Sir. Do you think he got out?
I think he went out the way he came in. Through the front door, with everyone else.
He looks along the road. At the far end, among the evacuees boarding the last bus, one of the figures turns his head and smiles. The bus pulls away.
INT. UNDERGROUND WORKSHOP, MADHAVARAM STAGE - NIGHT

The workshop, deep under the hill. A long bench has become a wall of phones, hundreds of them, wired in rows, each with a tiny green light. BRUCE WAYNE stands at the centre in a work shirt, his face gaunt, his hands black with solder.
FOX comes down the stairs with a roll of drawings under his arm. He looks at the wall and does not speak for a moment.
Is this what I think it is?
It is a listening net. Every phone in the city is also a microphone, if you can reach it.
Mr Wayne, that is an extraordinary piece of engineering and I would like it very much if you took it all down.
It is the only way to find him.
There are a million people in this city. You are going to listen to all of them.
It is not one night. A tool like that does not retire. It waits in a drawer until somebody else wants a night.
Bruce looks at the wall. The green lights ripple across it as signals pass.
I do not like it either.
A man has killed a judge and a policeman and burned a woman to death. He has destroyed a hospital. He intends to do it again, and again. Tell me what I should do instead.
I do not know. I only know I would not build it.
Fox sits on a stool and takes off his glasses. His hands are not quite steady.
On the wall of phones, a small green light blinks, then another. A faint murmur rises from the speakers, a thousand overlapping conversations rubbed down to a single soft hum, like surf.
Yes. And that is what troubles me. The moment I made it work, I knew I was going to be asked to run it.
You are asking me to be the person who stands next to a machine that hears everything and says nothing.
I am asking you to do it once.
I will do it once. And then I will resign.
It is not fair at all. It is the only thing left to me.
He puts on his glasses, takes his place at a console, and flips a row of switches. A tone rises in the cavern, thin and electric.
Whatever you hear, do not tell me. The more I know, the less I can forget.
On the screen, a single point of light blinks into life in the far south of the map. It does not stay still. It drifts, then stops, then drifts again.
I think that is your man.
Laughing. Very quietly. I think he is in a lift.
Police headquarters. The same long room, the fan still turning above a map of the whole city. Every constable in the building has been called in. They stand along the walls, in silence.
GORDON stands at the head, hoarse and unshaven. THE MAYOR sits beside him, hands clasped in his lap, face grey. RAMIREZ is at the telephones.
Sir. We have a message. It came in by radio, an hour ago. It was repeated three times.

"At midnight the city will be shut. People of means have already left. Those who have not are free to go. There are two ferries at the northern port, and a very small amount of time. One carries your honest citizens. The other carries your convicts. Each has a bomb, and each has a trigger on the other. If, at midnight, neither has been used, I will use them both."
A long silence in the room.
It is perfectly possible. He has had the whole week.
Then we will clear the ferries. Take everybody off.
He says the ferries are already wired. If anyone steps off, the charges will go.
Then we must evacuate the city a different way.
By what, sir? The bridges? The railway?
We cannot let half a million people stay in their homes.
With respect, I think half a million people will remain in their homes whatever we say. The ones who are leaving are on the ferries.
And the ones who are not?
They are the people who have decided to stay and see what happens.
He takes a pen and draws a circle on the map around the harbour. A hundred constables watch him do it.
We take every police launch we have to the port. We keep them out of sight, a mile off. If something happens, we are close.
Then at midnight, we will know a little more about what it is he is trying to tell us.
What is he trying to tell us?
Gordon looks at the map. The pins and the threads, the long scars of streets.
That people are not who we hope they are. He has been saying it all week. The ferries are the only time he has said it to everyone at once.
He caps the pen. For a moment the room is silent except for the fan.
Get the launches. And someone find me a man who can swim.
EXT. ENNORE PORT, FERRY BERTH - NIGHT
Ennore port, a quarter to midnight. Cranes stand like sleeping animals against a cloud-flecked sky. Two old ferries lie side by side at the berth, their lights burning, their ramps drawn up.
On the pier, hundreds of people wait in lines: families with bundles, old men on suitcases, a woman with a caged parrot. A few police stand along the edge, uneasy, looking out to sea.
A vendor sells tea from a flask to anyone who will stop. A boy with a transistor radio turns the dial and finds only static and a hymn.
The harbour lamps burn orange on the oily water. Gulls wheel under the gantries, their cries thin and far away.
At the far end of the pier, a second line, shorter and quieter. Prisoners in grey uniforms, shuffled in pairs by guards, hands chained at the waist.
Boarding in ten minutes. Please keep your bags in front of you. There is room for everybody.
Is it true what they say about the bomb?
I have not been told about any bomb.
There is one on each of them. I heard it on the radio.
Then you heard the radio. Please keep moving, sir.
A young woman in a nurse's cardigan with a small boy holds up a boarding pass in a shaking hand.
It is the same boat I have driven for eleven years.
That is not what I asked.
The captain is silent for a moment. He takes the pass, tears it in half, and hands the nurse the stub.
It is as safe as anything is tonight.
At the head of the prisoners' line, the WARDEN, a heavy man with a cap and a clipboard, checks off names with a ballpoint on a string. His men march the grey column up the ramp of the second ferry.
Keep in line. Nobody is going to hurt you. Nobody. Hands on the rail.
A very tall prisoner at the back of the line studies the wire fence, the cranes, the patch of black water beyond. He does not look at the guards. His face is scarred from the jaw to the ear.
The first ferry's ramp comes down. Passengers shuffle forward. The little boy holds his mother's hand and counts the steps aloud.
Out on the black water, a mile off, a flotilla of police launches sits in darkness, engines off. Gordon stands on the first, raising field glasses.
The ramps retract. Engines turn. The two ferries pull away from the pier, one behind the other, into the long sweep of harbour light.
On the pier, the police stand with their backs to the city and their faces to the sea, and nobody remarks on it.
The wake of the first ferry spreads in long white wings. The second follows it, black and low, with a single light burning at the stern.
INT. ENNORE PORT, PASSENGER FERRY - NIGHT

The main deck of the passenger ferry, long and low, wooden benches in rows, a stack of life jackets near the stairs. A hundred passengers sit shoulder to shoulder in the strip lighting, bags on their laps, eyes on the dark windows.
The engine thrums. Nobody speaks. A baby fusses a few rows back, and is soothed.
A shout from the stairs. A young crewman has found something: a flat grey box with a coiled wire, wedged under a bench. It has a green button and a small red switch, and a note taped to the lid.
"This is the trigger for the other boat. The one on the other boat is the trigger for yours. At midnight, whoever holds one may use it, or both will be used for them."
The deck falls silent. A man in a suit gets to his feet, pale, one hand over his mouth.
It is a joke. It has to be a joke.
There is another note on the back. It says we have a little over twenty minutes.
Then we should vote. We have to vote.
A rising murmur. Somebody laughs, high and nervous. A woman near the front begins to cry.
How can you say that? Press it, and the other ferry goes up. They are our own people.
They are criminals. The ones on the other boat are murderers and thieves.
Some of them are only men who failed to pay a fine.
And some of them are the people who put us on this boat.
The FERRY CAPTAIN comes down the stairs, hat in hand, breathing hard. He looks at the box, at the crowd, and at the clock over the door.
I want everyone to be calm. I have not heard anybody here say they will do anything.
