Captain, we have twenty minutes. Please. A vote.
A vote is a choice, sir. I do not think any of us is able to make this one.
You think we should do nothing?
I think nothing is the only thing that is honest.
And if the other side acts first?
Then they act first. And we will know what they were.
The crowd mutters. A knot of men gathers around the box. The suited man reaches for the button, and a hand closes on his wrist.
It is the nurse in the cardigan. The boy is on her hip, wide-eyed.
I have been in an emergency ward for ten years. You do not choose who comes in. You only choose whether you stay.
She does not move. A long silence. Then the suited man pulls his arm free, slowly, and sits down on the bench.
I do not know how you can be so sure.
I am not sure. I am only here.
The captain turns to the box. He lifts it, carries it to the rail, and throws it over the side. It vanishes in the black water without a splash.
There is no flash. No sound. The boat's engine thrums on.
I do not know. But we have still got the boat.
INT. ENNORE PORT, PRISONER FERRY - NIGHT

The lower deck of the prisoner ferry, a bare steel hold with long benches and iron rings in the floor. Forty men in grey sit shackled in rows. Six guards stand at the stairs, truncheons in their belts, eyes on the porthole.
The WARDEN holds a grey box in both hands. He does not seem to know where to put it. A note is stuck to the lid.
"Each of you can choose. A hundred and fifty innocent people on the other boat. Forty men of the opposite kind on this one. The first to act will be spared."
A ripple among the prisoners. One of the guards laughs, and is not joined.
It is a trick. They will blow us up either way.
What do you care? They put the bomb down here, not up there.
The tall prisoner with the scarred face, PRISONER ONE, speaks without raising his voice.
Give me the box and I will take care of it.
The guards stir. Two reach for their belts. The Warden raises a hand, stopping them, and looks the big man in the eye.
You have the worst file of any man on this boat.
You killed a man with a hammer.
Not a man. A hammer. I used the other thing to kill the man.
Is that supposed to be funny?
No. I only want you to know I am honest about what I did.
The Warden says nothing. The boat rolls. A prisoner at the end of the row begins, quietly, to pray.
I will tell you what I think, since you will not ask. Whoever put this on your boat is the one who put it on theirs. He wants one of us to press it. He does not mind which.
And you are going to be the one who does not?
I am going to be the one who makes sure nobody does. Give it here.
A long moment. The Warden looks at the box, then at the hundred small round faces of the men watching, and finally at his own guards. They look away.
He holds out the box. The tall man takes it in both hands, the chains between his wrists clinking.
He walks to the porthole. A guard starts forward, and the Warden stops him with a hand on his arm. The prisoner unlatches the glass.
That is my work for the evening.
He drops the box out of the porthole and into the sea. It falls without a sound.
The prisoners are silent. A guard on the stairs lets out a long, wet, shaking breath. The Warden takes off his cap and wipes his forehead with his sleeve.
A small sound at the back. A young prisoner, hardly more than a boy, has put his head down on his knees and is rocking slowly, and the man beside him has put an arm round him without a word.
The engine note drops a half-tone as the ferry comes about, and all forty heads turn together to the porthole, where a thin silver line has begun to show on the water.
He returns to his seat. The engine thrums. Overhead, the clock on the wall ticks to twelve.
An unfinished tower in Sholinganallur, forty storeys of bare concrete and scaffolding, black against a city that is mostly dark. No glass, no lifts, a wind that goes straight through.

On the thirtieth floor, a hundred feet of open floor, rows of columns, cables dangling from the ceiling. A dozen men in clown masks pace the floor with rifles. Beside them, huddled against a wall, ten people in hospital scrubs, hands tied.
A shape comes up the stairwell, a small flicker of green light on the wall as a pair of lenses catches the glow of a work lamp. BATMAN steps on to the floor and stops.
He sees them. He sees the masked men and the men in scrubs and the shadow of the stairs behind them. His visor sweeps across the room, tinting every face a pale blue.
A faint pulse of sound, sonar, and the walls draw themselves in pale lines around him: columns, stairs, beams, people. On the screen inside the cowl, a spray of heat tags. Twenty-two bodies.
It is him. Look. He has come.
Please. You do not have to do this. We are all hospital staff.
Batman holds up a hand. Twelve masked men, ten others. The pale lines sort them into two groups, and a third. Some of the masked men are hunched. Some of the scrubs are standing very still.

A cable sways overhead. A bucket of wet cement drips at one corner of the floor, ticking like a clock. Outside the open frames, the wind pulls a long flap of tarpaulin out into the sky and lets it snap back.
In the green glow of his lenses, a pair of boots shifts on the staircase behind him. He does not turn his head.
He takes a breath. Beside him, on the wall, a small fire extinguisher hangs from its hook. He lifts it down.
I am going to count to three. When I reach it, get down.
He throws the extinguisher across the floor. It hits a column with a bang and breaks open in a long white cloud. A burst of shouts. Rifles fire into the foam.
Batman is among the men before the cloud thins. He moves between them like a pair of scissors. A rifle butt, a shoulder, a leg. A man spins into a column.
Two of the people in scrubs rise. They are not hostages. They pull rifles from under the scrubs and aim at Batman's back. He ducks and rolls, and the rifles blast a line of holes in the wall.
I told you. They are dressed the wrong way round.
A masked man takes him from behind in a chokehold. Batman drives an elbow into his stomach and flips him over his shoulder. The man's mask comes off.
Underneath is a surgeon's cap and a hospital badge. He is one of the real hostages. He is weeping.
The next masked man is a real masked man. Batman puts him through a window of bare concrete. Below, forty floors of nothing.
The man hangs from a rod, kicking at the air, and a hostage in scrubs hauls him back inside by the belt. Neither seems quite able to say what has happened.
Two more come at Batman from the left. He catches the first one's rifle by the barrel and swings it into the second's chest. They go down together in a tangle of cloth and cables.
On the ceiling above him a grey rope swings down. The Joker's voice, from somewhere in the dark, high and bright.
Do you see? They are all so much alike. It is the clothes that make the difference.
Batman looks up. In the cloud of foam, a purple shape drops to a crouch on a girder, laughing.
The roof of the tower. Cold, open sky, a few stars. The edge is a rough line of rebar and scaffold poles. Below, a long drop, then the grey sea of the city.
BATMAN and the JOKER, face to face, ten feet apart. Smoke from the floor below drifts between them. In the far distance, a faint grey light begins to rise in the east.
You are an hour late. The ferries are done.
Neither boat. Not one man on either.
The Joker's smile freezes at its edges. For a moment, the paint looks like a painting of a smile.
That is not possible. I know them. I have studied them very carefully.
It is a mistake. A small clerical error. The numbers will correct themselves.
I have made a very good argument. Everyone I meet is a case for it. They would sell each other for a ticket. They are no better than I am.
You said you wanted to prove something to me.
And you have. Just not what you intended.
The Joker takes a long breath and lets it out. His shoulders drop an inch. Then he lunges.
He swings a length of pipe at Batman's head. Batman blocks it with a forearm, takes it from him, throws it into the dark. They grapple, boot on rebar, two black shapes on the roof's grey edge.
The Joker twists, pulls a thin knife from his coat. Batman catches his wrist and holds it. They struggle against the wind.
Go on. Do it. You are not allowed to.
He snaps the wrist and the knife drops. The Joker howls, then laughs. He staggers back across the lip of the roof, laughing at the stars.
Look at us. A very sad little pair.
His heel hits the rebar. He tips back. Batman lunges and catches him by the ankle. For a second they hang there, one man holding another over the whole dark city.
From the stairwell, a roar of boots. Gordon and fifty policemen burst on to the roof, torches blazing.
Batman shifts his grip, hauls the Joker up and drops him on the concrete, a tangle of purple. The Joker lies on his back, shaking with laughter, tears in the paint.
It is such a good joke. I am afraid nobody else will get it.
Gordon stands over him with a pair of handcuffs. He looks at Batman, who steps back to the edge, and for a moment says nothing.
I held him. It is not the same.
I will take it from here.
I know. I wish I could say it ended better.
The grey light grows in the east. The Joker's laughter goes on. The cuffs close.
INT. GORDON'S HOUSE, BESANT NAGAR - NIGHT
A modest house in Besant Nagar, a living room with a ceiling fan and a plastic sofa. A photograph of a wedding, a cricket bat in the corner. A single lamp.
MRS GORDON sits at the end of the sofa, a cold cup of tea beside her, hands folded. GORDON'S SON, nine years old in school uniform, is doing his homework at the table by the window.
Amma, why is there no news?
Because it is late and the news people are asleep.
Appa is at work. He will be home when it is finished.
The boy watches her with narrowed eyes, then looks down at his page. He writes a word and rubs it out.
I do not think he is at work.
Because when he is at work, he rings.
She does not answer. A key in the door. They both turn.
Gordon comes in, his arm in a sling, his uniform torn, his face grey. He stops on the threshold.
I am a little the worse. But I am alive.
She gets up. She walks across the floor, quite slowly, and puts both arms round him, careful of the sling. He holds her with the good one.
The boy comes over, stops half a step away, uncertain.
A little. I fell off a roof.
There was a lot of bad weather up there.
He sinks to one knee, so his face is level with the boy's. The boy touches the sling with a small finger.
Did you catch the bad man?
Not all of it. But the worst, I think.
Mrs Gordon smooths her husband's collar. She sees the soot on it, the torn button, and a purple card sticking from the pocket.
She takes the card out and looks at it. She folds it, very small, and puts it in the pocket of her own apron.
Come and sit. I will make you something to eat.
I do not think I could eat.
Then you will sit with us while we do.
He lets her lead him to the sofa. The boy brings his homework and sits against his father's good side, and for a minute the room is only a lamp and a fan.
A half-built tenement block in Royapuram, five storeys of bare concrete and rusted rods, the stairs still without rails. A wind comes straight through the empty window frames.

On the third floor, in a room with a single lantern, a chair has been set against the wall. MRS GORDON sits in it. GORDON'S SON stands on the other side, a hand on her arm. They are not tied. They do not seem to need to be.

HARVEY DENT stands at the window with his back to them. His coat is scorched, a bandage half off, one side of his face a ruin of raw tissue and one eye wide and clear. A silver coin turns on his knuckles.
Gordon comes up the stairs with a pistol held low, his sling gone. He stops in the doorway, quite out of breath.
I will. But first I would like you to understand what it is like. To stand in a place like this and have everything decided for you by a coin.
You are not a man who throws coins.
I am now. It is a very quiet way to live. It asks nothing and promises nothing and it is always right.
It is a piece of silver.
It is a reasonable judge. Which is more than I can say for the others.
He turns round. Mrs Gordon gasps. The boy does not look away.
Hello, child. You were very small when we met. You have not changed.
A noise at the other end of the floor. A boot on concrete. BATMAN, in the doorway, silent, with his arms at his sides.
And here is my other friend. Such a busy night.
It is exactly me. It is the first time I have been exactly me. All those years in the court, being fair. And what did fair do for her?
Then why should I be fair now?
He holds up the coin. In the lantern light it glints once.
I will let it decide. One flip for you, one for the family, one for me. If it falls the right way, the person lives.
He flips it. It rises, spins, catches the light. He does not look at it. His eyes are on Gordon.
You should have kept her safe.
The coin lands. He picks it up. He shows it to nobody.
Batman rushes him. Dent turns and swings the pistol round. The shot is deafening, and Batman is thrown against the wall.
Gordon fires. Dent is hit and spun. He stumbles, grabs the edge of a window frame. Below him there is only air.
Dent looks at the boy. For a moment the clear eye and the ruined one are both full of the same thing. Then the window frame gives way, and he falls.
Silence. Wind through the empty windows. Far below, a small sound that is not a sound.
Batman gets up slowly from the floor, clutching his ribs. Gordon has gone to the window. The boy buries his face in his mother's dress.

The pavement outside the tenement, a moment after. A long wall of concrete and a patch of rubble. At its foot, HARVEY DENT lies on his back, quite still, one hand open. The silver coin lies in the dust a foot from it.
Police lights flicker on the walls. A constable is stringing tape across the road. In the shadow of the wall, BATMAN stands beside GORDON, both looking down.
Gordon kneels. He lays two fingers at Dent's throat, then takes them away.
What are we going to say to people?
The truth. A good man died, and then he did not.
They will want somebody to blame.
All of them. Dent's deaths and the ones before. The people need to go on believing in him. If they do not, the last year will have been for nothing.
You cannot ask that of yourself.
It is not what I am asking. It is what I am prepared to do.
Gordon looks away. Behind the tape, a crowd has gathered: office workers, auto drivers, a woman with a shopping bag. A boy's face, glimpsed between two men, looks over the barrier at Batman.
Gordon stands. He picks up the silver coin and turns it over in his palm. He holds it out to Batman.
No. Put it somewhere it cannot decide anything.
Gordon slips the coin into his pocket. A siren rises. He puts a hand on the cape and holds on a moment longer than he should.
I will tell them what you said. The part about him being good.
It is the only part that matters.
He steps back. The wall is a long blank grey, with a gap at the end where the rubble forms a ramp. Batman climbs it without a sound.
At the top, he looks down once at the crowd, the tape, the policemen, the man in the road. He does not say goodbye.
Gordon watches him go. The boy at the barrier lifts a hand halfway, as if to wave, and lowers it again when nobody else does.
A cold breeze lifts the tape and sets it humming.
He is gone before the first reporter's flash goes off.

A river road in Adyar, long and nearly empty, a line of tamarind trees along the water. A grey dawn is breaking over the city. A few early cyclists, an auto with its lights still on, a milkman on a bicycle.

GORDON stands on the road in his torn overcoat. Beside him, RAMIREZ holds a loudhailer she has forgotten to use. A line of police cars has stopped at the bend. Every constable is looking at the same thing.
At the end of the road, a black bike. On it, a dark figure, quite still. The engine idles.
He is not going to run.
Yes. It is the one I have to give.
He takes the loudhailer. He holds it a moment and then lowers it. Behind him, a car door opens. A constable gets out, staring at the bike.
The man on the road is wanted in connection with the death of a prosecutor. All units, stand ready. He is armed and dangerous.
A murmur among the constables. They glance at each other. A dozen engines start.
I mean every word. And I will say it again tomorrow. And I will go on saying it until one of us dies.
Because the city has to believe it. And somebody has to make them.
The bike turns its head toward the line of police cars. For an instant the two faces, the cowl and the officer's, are exactly level.

Then the engine opens up in a long soft snarl, the front wheel lifts, and the bike goes up the river road into the dawn. The police cars give chase, their sirens rising. They are never going to catch him.
Gordon lowers the loudhailer. He stands alone on the empty road for a long moment, looking after the engine's fading note.

Behind him the police cars are lining up at the bend with their engines idling and nobody giving the order to move. The constables stand in the road or lean on the doors, looking at the same empty stretch of tarmac.
A milkman, forgotten, pulls his bicycle to the verge and takes off his cap.
On the water, the first sun touches a flat of grey ripples and turns it, for a moment, to gold.
He takes the silver coin from his pocket and weighs it. He tosses it high, in a slow arc. It falls into the river and does not make a sound.
